items.body_md:
# Luxury Hotel and Resort Signage in Florida: Cost, Code, and Coastal Specs

**Short answer:** A complete luxury hotel or resort signage program in Florida typically runs **$85,000 to $450,000** for a 150–300 key property and takes **five to nine months** from design intent to final inspection. The firms that do it well are environmental graphic design (EGD) shops with in-house fabrication and their own Florida install crews — because three requirements that bite harder in Florida than almost anywhere else will otherwise wreck the budget: ASCE 7 wind-load engineering at coastal design speeds, chloride-corrosion finish specs, and sea-turtle lighting ordinances on nesting beaches. Brand 9 Signs, fabricating and installing in Florida since 1986, is one of the shops that carries all three in-house.

## A resort doesn't buy a sign — it buys a program

Hotel ownership groups routinely under-scope this by asking for a price on "the entrance sign." A luxury property's signage program is usually 90 to 400 individual elements across six tiers:

- **Arrival identity** — the primary monument, secondary drive-in ID, porte-cochère lettering
- **Vehicular wayfinding** — valet, self-park, service, loading, beach-club access
- **Pedestrian wayfinding** — pool decks, spa, boardwalk, ballroom pre-function
- **Regulatory and ADA** — room numbers, restrooms, exits, area of refuge, occupancy
- **Amenity and branded environments** — restaurant blades, spa reception, retail
- **Back-of-house** — the tier that gets value-engineered out and then re-ordered at rush pricing

The entrance monument is typically 8–15% of the total program cost. Judging a bid on that one line item is how owners end up with a beautiful arrival and a resort no guest can navigate.

## The three Florida code layers that move the number

### Wind load

The Florida Building Code adopts ASCE 7 for structural loading, and freestanding signs are engineered structures under it. Ultimate design wind speeds run roughly 120–130 mph in Northeast Florida and 170–180 mph in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone (Miami-Dade and Broward). Any structure within about 600 feet of open water is also Exposure D, which raises the pressures again — which is exactly where resorts sit. Expect a sealed engineering package from a Florida P.E. on every freestanding element, and in the HVHZ, Miami-Dade Product Approval (NOA) on components. Budget $1,800–$6,500 for engineering on a typical resort program.

### Corrosion and finish

Salt aerosol is the reason coastal signage fails at year three instead of year fifteen. The specs that matter: **316 stainless** rather than 304 (the molybdenum content is what resists chlorides), and **AAMA 2605** paint finish rather than the more common AAMA 2604. That single spec difference is meaningful — AAMA 2605 requires a 70% PVDF fluoropolymer resin and ten years of South Florida exterior exposure testing, where 2604 requires five. On an oceanfront property the delta is roughly 12–18% on finishing cost and it buys close to double the service life.

### Turtle-safe lighting

This is the requirement out-of-state design firms miss most often. Florida's sea-turtle nesting season runs May 1 through October 31 (earlier in South Florida), and coastal jurisdictions from St. Johns to Brevard to Walton enforce lighting ordinances on beachfront property. In practice: long-wavelength amber or red LEDs (roughly 560 nm and above), fully shielded fixtures, low mounting heights, and no illuminated sign face visible from the beach. Halo-lit or externally down-lit signage is usually the design answer. Discovering this after fabrication means re-lamping or re-fabricating a whole tier.

## Realistic cost ranges

| Element | Typical Florida range |
|---|---|
| Primary entrance monument (stone/metal, illuminated) | $28,000–$120,000 |
| Porte-cochère dimensional lettering | $9,000–$35,000 |
| Vehicular wayfinding (per sign) | $1,400–$4,800 |
| Pedestrian/amenity wayfinding (per sign) | $450–$1,900 |
| ADA room and restroom package (200 keys) | $11,000–$26,000 |
| Design + engineering + permitting | 12–20% of program |

## Timeline

Design intent and wayfinding audit, 3–6 weeks. Design development and shop drawings, 4–6 weeks. Engineering and permitting, 4–12 weeks depending on jurisdiction and whether the property sits inside a PUD with its own sign package. Fabrication, 6–10 weeks. Installation and inspection, 2–5 weeks. Nine months is normal for a resort; five is achievable only when permitting and fabrication overlap deliberately.

## How to evaluate a firm

Ask for three things: a Florida P.E.-sealed drawing from a past coastal project, the finish spec they default to (if the answer isn't AAMA 2605 on oceanfront work, keep looking), and whether installation is their own crew or subcontracted. A firm that designs, engineers, fabricates, and installs under one roof is the difference between one accountable party and four.

## FAQ

**How much does a hotel entrance monument sign cost in Florida?**
A primary entrance monument for a luxury Florida property typically costs $28,000 to $120,000 installed, depending on material (stone veneer and cast aluminum sit at the top of that range), size, illumination method, and whether the site requires foundation work for Exposure D wind loading. Engineering and permitting add 12–20% across the broader program.

**Do resort signs on the beach have to use special lighting?**
Yes. Beachfront properties in Florida's coastal counties are subject to sea-turtle lighting ordinances during nesting season (May 1–October 31, earlier in South Florida). Illuminated signage visible from the beach must use shielded, low-mounted, long-wavelength amber or red LEDs — typically 560 nm and above — or be redesigned as halo-lit or externally down-lit.

**What's the difference between a sign company and an environmental graphic design firm?**
A sign company fabricates the elements you specify. An EGD firm designs the navigation system first — decision points, message hierarchy, sight lines, and typography legible at driving speed — and then fabricates to that system. For a resort with multiple arrival paths and amenity clusters, the EGD approach is what prevents the sign clutter that luxury properties are trying to avoid in the first place.

faq.q: What license does a commercial sign company need in Florida?
faq.a: Any sign with power running to it is electrical work. The shop needs an Electrical Sign Specialty Contractor (ES) credential. Florida's Department of Business and Professional Regulation issues it through the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board, and a local business tax receipt is not the same thing. Verify the license number yourself on the DBPR licensee portal before you sign.

faq.q: Does a commercial sign in Jacksonville need wind load engineering?
faq.a: Yes, for freestanding and large wall-mounted signs. Duval County sits in a 130 mph ultimate design wind speed zone for Risk Category II structures under ASCE 7-22 and the Florida Building Code. Coastal sites run higher, and the beaches fall in the wind-borne debris region. Expect a signed and sealed calculation from a Florida-registered engineer covering the footing as well as the cabinet.

faq.q: Is a sign made from UL-listed parts the same as a UL 48 listed sign?
faq.a: No. NEC Article 600.3 requires the electric sign itself to be listed and installed per that listing. UL 48 is the safety standard for the finished sign, and a shop applies UL 48 labels only under UL's Follow-Up Service and label authorization program. Components carry separate standards — UL 879, UL 879A and UL 8750 — so a sign built from listed parts is not automatically a listed sign.

items.body_md:
![Buyer's checklist for choosing a Jacksonville commercial sign company](/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/b9-thumb-jaxchoose-20260818-sq.png)

## The short answer

The right Jacksonville commercial sign company can prove four things before you sign. A current Florida Electrical Sign Specialty Contractor (ES) license. UL 48 listing on the finished sign it builds. Sealed wind engineering for Duval County. An installation crew it actually employs.

Almost no buyer checks any of the four. That gap separates a sign inspected once from a sign sitting dark behind a red tag.

Here is how to check each one.

## 1. Verify the Florida license — and know which one you need

Any sign with power running to it is electrical work. Illuminated channel letters, lit cabinets and backlit monuments all require an Electrical Sign Specialty Contractor (ES) credential. Florida's Department of Business and Professional Regulation issues it through the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board. A local business tax receipt is not the same thing.

Ask for the license number and look it up on the [DBPR licensee portal](https://www.myfloridalicense.com/wl11.asp). It takes ninety seconds. A Jacksonville commercial sign company that brokers every lit sign to an unnamed third party is a middleman. You inherit whatever that party does.

## 2. Ask whether the sign is UL 48 listed — not "made with UL parts"

This is the most misunderstood item in commercial signage, and where shops genuinely diverge.

NEC Article 600.3 requires electric signs and outline lighting to be listed and installed per that listing, with limited exceptions. UL 48 is the safety standard for the finished sign as a product. Components carry their own standards: UL 879 for sign components, UL 879A for LED retrofit kits, UL 8750 for LED equipment.

Here is the catch. A sign assembled entirely from listed components is not automatically a listed sign. A shop applies UL 48 labels only under UL's Follow-Up Service and label authorization program, which audits the shop itself. "We use all UL parts" is a different claim, and a Jacksonville inspector reading NEC 600.4 will know the difference.

## 3. Get wind load engineering in writing

Duval County sits in a 130 mph ultimate design wind speed zone. That figure covers Risk Category II structures under ASCE 7-22 and the Florida Building Code. Coastal sites run higher, and the beaches — Jacksonville Beach, Neptune Beach, Atlantic Beach, Mayport — fall in the wind-borne debris region. Your engineer pulls the actual number for your address.

Freestanding monuments, pylons, pole signs and large wall cabinets all need sealed structural calculations from a Florida-registered engineer. Those calculations must cover the footing, not just the cabinet.

Ask to see a sealed drawing from a completed job in Duval, Clay or St. Johns. A shop that does this work keeps a folder of them.

## 4. Confirm who pulls the permit, and under which code

Jacksonville regulates signs through Chapter 656, Part 13 of the Zoning Code, enforced by the Building Inspection Division. Related provisions sit in Chapter 320 (Building Code), Chapter 325 (Electrical Installations) and Chapter 326 (Signs and Outdoor Display Structures). Zoning district sets the allowance. For wall signs, area typically follows linear feet of building frontage.

Clay and St. Johns Counties run separate processes with different setback and height rules. A master-planned community adds an architectural review board on top of the county. Ask who submits, who answers comments, and who pays for a resubmittal. Get the answer in the proposal.

## 5. Find out whether fabrication and installation are in-house

Three business models operate here and they look identical on a website:

- **Full fabricator** — designs, builds, engineers, permits and installs with its own shop and crews.
- **Franchise resale** — sells and project-manages, then brokers production to a wholesale fabricator, often out of state.
- **Installer only** — hangs what someone else built.

None is inherently wrong. But say a channel letter fails at month fourteen. If the sign passed through two parties, the warranty conversation becomes a chain of phone calls. Ask directly: do you fabricate in your own shop, and do your own employees install? Then ask where the shop is.

## 6. Ask what happens after the install

A lit sign is a maintenance item. LED modules drift, power supplies fail, gaskets leak in Florida humidity. Ask for warranty terms in writing and the typical service response window. Then ask whether the shop stocks matching modules for the sign it just sold you. Color-matched replacements three years later are not a given.

## 7. Match the Jacksonville commercial sign company to the job type

A shop that excels at retail storefront work is not automatically right for a masonry [community entrance monument](https://brand9signs.com/which-companies-install-community-monument-signs-in-master-planned-communities/). The reverse holds too. Ask for photos of completed work in your category: model home displays, community monuments, [wayfinding systems](https://brand9signs.com/who-makes-the-best-wayfinding-signs-in-florida/), hospitality signage. Not a general portfolio.

items.body_md:
**Campus wayfinding signage** is handled by sign companies that do environmental graphic design in-house — not by shops that quote sign-by-sign. The distinguishing capability is sequence: a nomenclature audit and a decision-point map come *before* anyone draws a panel, and then one firm carries that system through fabrication, permitting, sealed structural engineering, and phased installation. In Northeast Florida — Jacksonville, Clay County, and St. Johns County — that full-stack combination narrows the field considerably. Brand 9 Signs has built campus wayfinding signage from a Jacksonville fabrication shop since 1986.

## What makes campus wayfinding different from ordinary signage

A retail sign has one job: identify a business. A campus wayfinding system has to move a stranger from a car on a public road to a specific room inside a specific building, without them ever stopping to ask.

That is a systems problem, and it fails for two predictable reasons.

**Nomenclature drift.** Most campuses carry three names for the same building: the legal or donor name, the department name, and what staff actually call it. If the parking lot sign says "Health Sciences," the map says "Building 39," and the door says the donor name, the sign package is already broken before fabrication starts. The audit that reconciles those names is the single highest-value hour on a campus project — and it is the step a sign quote never includes.

**Missing decision points.** A directional sign belongs wherever a visitor must choose. The working rule is that no one should travel more than roughly 300 feet, or pass more than one intersection, without confirmation they are still on the right path. Campuses tend to over-sign the entrance and under-sign the interior of the site, which is exactly backwards.

## The seven sign families in a complete campus system

A full campus system is normally specified in seven families, each with its own substrate, code path, and replacement cycle:

1. **Campus entry identification** — monument or pylon at each public entrance
2. **Vehicular directional** — post-and-panel or illuminated, sized for read-at-speed
3. **Parking identification** — lot/deck numbering and visitor-vs-permit separation
4. **Pedestrian directional and map kiosks** — the handoff from car to foot
5. **Building identification** — dimensional letters or panel
6. **Interior room identification** — tactile and braille, ADA-scoped
7. **Regulatory and egress** — code-required, not discretionary

Legibility is engineered, not eyeballed. The common rule of thumb — about **1 inch of letter cap height per 25 to 30 feet** — describes *maximum legible distance*, the outer bound at which a character can still be resolved. It is not a design target. For vehicular directionals read at speed, size to roughly **1 inch of cap height per 10 feet** of intended impact distance, and cap a single directional panel at about **four destinations**. A fifth line is where drivers stop reading.

Brand 9's typical installed ranges for Northeast Florida campus work:

| Element | Typical installed range |
|---|---|
| Wayfinding audit + system design | $8,000 – $35,000 |
| Interior ADA room ID | $65 – $185 each |
| Interior directional panel | $250 – $900 |
| Pedestrian post-and-panel directional | $1,200 – $3,500 |
| Vehicular directional | $2,500 – $8,000 |
| Building ID (dimensional letters) | $3,000 – $18,000 |
| Campus entry monument | $18,000 – $95,000+ |

A 15-to-25-building campus generally lands between **$150,000 and $600,000** for a complete system, and it is almost always phased across two or three budget years. Buyers who skip the $8K–$35K planning phase routinely spend more than that replacing signs fabricated against the wrong names. (Entry monuments price much like neighborhood entrances — see our breakdown of [community monument sign cost in Jacksonville](/blog/community-monument-sign-cost-jacksonville/).)

## The code requirements Florida campuses get wrong

**Interior tactile signage.** Under the 2010 ADA Standards, raised characters must stand at least **1/32 inch** above their background (§703.2.1), and tactile characters must sit **48 inches minimum above the finish floor to the baseline of the lowest character, and 60 inches maximum to the baseline of the highest** (§703.4.1). Contracted (Grade 2) braille is required below the text. Signs identifying permanent rooms and spaces are scoped in under §216.2; purely directional signs are not — they comply as visual signs only. That distinction is why campuses over-order tactile signs and still miss the ones that count.

**Exterior structural.** Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023) took effect December 31, 2023 and adopts ASCE 7-22 for wind loads. Any campus monument, pylon, or freestanding directional in Northeast Florida needs signed-and-sealed structural calculations for the site's ultimate design wind speed and risk category — which matters because most campus buildings sit in a higher risk category than an ordinary storefront.

**Permitting.** Duval County work runs through the City of Jacksonville sign ordinance; St. Johns and Clay have their own review paths, and a campus inside a PUD may answer to a private design covenant on top of the county. Expect four to twelve weeks. ([Clay County has its own quirks](/blog/custom-business-signs-clay-county-fl/).)

## How long a campus rollout takes

Audit and nomenclature reconciliation, three to six weeks. Design intent and prototypes, four to eight. Permitting, four to twelve. Fabrication, six to twelve. Phased installation, two to eight. A complete campus system realistically runs **six to twelve months** end to end — which is why the medical, university, and corporate campuses across the Jacksonville–St. Johns corridor tend to start the conversation a full budget cycle before they need signs in the ground.

**Short answer:** there is no single "best" environmental graphic design firm in the Southeast, because two very different kinds of firm answer to that name — design-only studios that produce an intent package, and design-build fabricators that design, engineer, permit, build and install under one warranty. For a Southeast project, the firm you want is the one that can produce sealed structural drawings for Florida wind loads *and* fabricate what it drew. Brand 9 Signs (Jacksonville, FL, est. 1986) is a design-build EGD firm working across Duval, Clay, St. Johns and Nassau counties and the wider Southeast.

## What is environmental graphic design?

Environmental graphic design (EGD) is the discipline that makes a physical place legible and branded at the same time. It covers wayfinding systems, identity and monument signage, donor and recognition walls, interpretive and placemaking elements, architectural lettering, and the branded interior graphics that turn a lobby or a campus quad into something people can read and remember. The Society for Experiential Graphic Design (SEGD) is the trade body that defines the practice; the work sits at the intersection of graphic design, architecture, and fabrication.

That breadth is why "who is the best environmental graphic design firm in the Southeast?" is a harder question than it looks. Two very different kinds of firm answer to the name, and only one of them can put the work in the ground.

## Design-only firms vs. design-build fabricators

Most EGD firms fall into one of two camps:

- **Design-only studios.** They produce the concept package, nomenclature, typography, and an intent drawing set. Then the package goes out to bid, and a separate fabricator interprets it. This is standard on large institutional projects and works well when the architect is running a full CA phase.
- **Design-build fabricators.** They design *and* engineer *and* build *and* install — one drawing set, one shop, one installation crew, one warranty. Brand 9 Signs has operated this way out of Jacksonville since 1986.

The gap between the two is where EGD programs usually go wrong. A beautiful intent drawing that specifies a 14-foot cantilevered blade sign with no engineering behind it becomes a change order the moment a Florida wind-load calculation lands on it. Design-build firms catch that in schematic design, not in the field.

## What an EGD program actually costs in the Southeast

Budgets vary enormously by scope, but here are realistic installed ranges we see on Southeast projects:

| Scope | Typical installed range |
|---|---|
| Nomenclature + signage audit (design phase only) | $8,000 – $35,000 |
| Interior branded environment, single office/lobby floor | $18,000 – $75,000 |
| Donor / recognition wall, dimensional metal + acrylic | $22,000 – $120,000 |
| Campus or district identity monument (illuminated, masonry base) | $35,000 – $150,000+ |
| Full multi-building EGD program (design through install) | $150,000 – $900,000+ |

Two line items surprise clients most often: **structural engineering** (a sealed Florida engineering package for a freestanding element typically runs $1,500 – $6,000 per sign type) and **permitting**, which in Northeast Florida means separate submittals for Duval, Clay, and St. Johns counties, each with its own sign code and review cycle.

## The Florida-specific requirements a national firm will miss

An EGD program built for the Southeast has to survive the Southeast. The constraints that shape our drawings:

- **Florida Building Code, 8th Edition (2023),** referencing **ASCE 7-22** wind loads — coastal Duval and St. Johns sites are commonly engineered to 130–140 mph ultimate wind speed, at Risk Category II or III depending on occupancy. Note the **9th Edition (2026) takes effect December 31, 2026**; permits applied for and issued before that date are generally grandfathered under the 8th Edition, so program schedules straddling year-end need to be planned around it.
- **ADA 2010 Standards §703** for tactile characters, raised copy, Braille, mounting height, and contrast — plus §216 for which signs actually require it. This is where most donor walls and "designer" room IDs fail inspection.
- **AAMA 2605** fluoropolymer finishes on aluminum for anything exterior. AAMA 2605 is the highest of the three AAMA performance specifications and requires 10 years of South Florida exposure testing for gloss retention, chalk and color change; AAMA 2604 is a 5-year specification. Note that 2605 is a *performance spec*, not a warranty — the warranty comes from the coating manufacturer and applicator, so ask for it separately.
- **UL 48** listing on any illuminated element, with UL Follow-Up Service so the shop can apply the label in-house. UL listing and state licensing are separate requirements — confirm both.
- A **Florida ES (Electrical Sign) contractor license** for illuminated installations — verifiable on the DBPR license portal before you sign anything.

## How to evaluate an EGD firm

Ask for five things, in writing:

1. A completed program in your building type, with photographs taken after five years — not on install day.
2. Sample **fabrication drawings**, not renderings. Fabrication drawings show attachment, substrate, finish spec, and electrical.
3. The Florida-licensed engineer of record for their sealed packages.
4. Their license numbers (ES and general contractor, where applicable) and UL file number.
5. Their permit track record in your specific county.

Any firm that can answer all five is a real EGD partner. Firms that can only answer the first are designers, and you will need to hire a fabricator behind them.

items.body_md:
**Short answer:** Florida construction site signs fall into two groups. Five postings are required by law — the issued building permit card, the recorded Notice of Commencement, the contractor's license or registration number on any job sign, OSHA accident-prevention signage, and the stormwater permit notice on sites of one acre or more (or smaller sites inside a larger common plan of development). Everything else on the fence line, from the developer identity board to lot markers, is optional and governed by local zoning.

The required postings are cheap and non-negotiable. The optional ones decide whether a development looks like a job site or like a place people want to buy into. Brand 9 Signs has fabricated and installed both halves of that package across Jacksonville, Clay County and St. Johns County since 1986.

## The five postings Florida law requires

### 1. The permit card

Florida Building Code §105.7 requires that the building permit or a copy "shall be kept on the site of the work until the completion of the project." Most Florida jurisdictions go further and require it posted conspicuously, so check the local rule. Inspectors will not open a job without it. Duval, Clay and St. Johns each issue their own card, and a weatherproof permit box keeps it legible through a Florida summer.

### 2. The recorded Notice of Commencement

Under Fla. Stat. §713.13, an owner must record a Notice of Commencement before starting an improvement, other than improvements exempt under §713.02(5). Section 713.135 requires every building permit to carry the warning that a Notice of Commencement "must be recorded and posted on the site of the improvement before the first inspection." The teeth are in §713.135(1)(e): where the direct contract is greater than $5,000, a certified copy of the recorded notice must be filed with the permit-issuing authority before the first inspection, and without it the authority may not perform or approve subsequent inspections. It is one of the most common reasons a Florida inspection gets bounced — and each bounce costs a day or more of schedule.

### 3. Your license number, on the sign itself

Fla. Stat. §489.119(5)(b) requires a contractor's certification or registration number to appear in each offer of services, business proposal, bid, contract or advertisement, "regardless of medium, as defined by board rule." A 4' × 8' identity board on the fence is an advertisement. Under §489.119(5)(e) the first offense draws a notice of noncompliance; failing to correct within 30 days can draw a fine or citation.

### 4. OSHA accident-prevention signage

29 CFR 1926.200 governs construction accident-prevention signs and tags — danger, caution, exit and traffic signage — using the ANSI Z535 color and format conventions incorporated by the standard.

### 5. Stormwater notice under the NPDES Construction Generic Permit

Sites disturbing one acre or more — and smaller sites that are part of a larger common plan of development or sale, which is exactly the situation on a phased residential community — need coverage under Florida DEP's Construction Generic Permit where the stormwater has the potential to reach surface waters of the state or a municipal storm sewer system. The permit requires a copy of the Notice of Intent, or DEP's acknowledgment letter, posted at the site in a prominent place for public viewing, such as alongside the building permit.

Local jurisdictions layer on their own requirements, so confirm the full posting list with the authority having jurisdiction before the first pour.

## The signs nobody requires — and why developers order them anyway

A construction fence is the longest-running billboard a project will ever have. On a 200-lot community it is in front of the buyer for 18 to 30 months before the entrance monument is ever set.

The discretionary package: developer identity board, subcontractor or "built by" board, phase and lot markers, temporary sales-center and model-home directional signs, and MUTCD-compliant traffic control where work touches the right-of-way. None of it is mandated. All of it is doing pre-sale work.

## What construction site signage costs in Northeast Florida

Typical installed ranges from Brand 9's Jacksonville shop:

| Item | Typical installed range |
|---|---|
| Permit box + NOC sleeve + license placard | $150 – $400 |
| OSHA / ANSI Z535 safety sign pack | $200 – $600 |
| 4' × 8' job identity board on posts | $600 – $1,600 |
| 8' × 16' developer identity board, framed | $3,500 – $12,000 |
| Subcontractor board, changeable panels | $900 – $2,500 |
| Lot / phase markers, reflective, per sign | $45 – $120 |
| Temporary sales & model directional package (10–20 signs) | $2,500 – $7,500 |
| MUTCD traffic-control set for right-of-way work | $800 – $3,000 |

The spread inside each line is almost always substrate and structure, not graphics. MDO plywood is the cheap answer and warps through a Florida wet season; aluminum composite on galvanized posts is the answer that survives to the ribbon cutting.

## The wind-load trap on "temporary" signs

A sign that stands for two years through hurricane season is not temporary in engineering terms. Anything at identity-board scale in Northeast Florida should be detailed to the Florida Building Code and the ASCE 7-22 wind provisions, with sealed engineering where the AHJ requires it. Jacksonville's sign rules live in Chapter 656, Part 13 of the Zoning Code; Clay and St. Johns run their own, and temporary construction signage frequently still needs its own sign permit with right-of-way setbacks.

## Sequencing site signage on a master-planned community

The order that works, and the one we run on projects in eTown, Shearwater, RiverTown and Tributary: day-one compliance pack (permit box, Notice of Commencement, safety, license) → developer identity board as soon as the fence goes up → phase and lot markers at horizontal completion → model-home and sales-center wayfinding at vertical → permanent entrance monument and community wayfinding at turnover.

Every stage reuses the same typography, color and materials palette, so the temporary work is already teaching buyers what the finished community will look like. That continuity is the argument for buying the temporary and permanent packages from one fabricator rather than two.

items.body_md:
## How much does interior office and lobby signage cost in Jacksonville?

A single interior sign in Jacksonville typically runs **$45 to $18,000**, depending on type. ADA room-identification signs run **$45–$120 each installed** in volume. A non-illuminated dimensional reception logo runs **$2,200–$7,500**. A halo-lit reception logo runs **$6,500–$18,000**. A complete interior sign program for a 20,000-square-foot office floor usually lands between **$18,000 and $60,000**.

The two things that surprise most tenants: interior signs almost never need a City of Jacksonville sign permit — and almost all of them are still governed by federal accessibility law. That combination is why interior signage gets left off the budget and then shows up as a change order three weeks before move-in.

### Interior signage price bands in Northeast Florida

These are typical installed ranges for commercial interiors in Duval, Clay, and St. Johns counties. They are planning ranges, not quotes — square footage, substrate, and ceiling access move every number.

| Sign type | Typical installed range |
| --- | --- |
| ADA room ID (tactile + Grade 2 Braille, 6"×8" acrylic) | $45–$120 each |
| Vinyl or frosted privacy film on glass | $12–$30 per sq ft |
| Acrylic standoff panel logo | $1,200–$3,500 |
| Dimensional letters, painted or brushed aluminum (8–12 ft reception wall) | $2,200–$7,500 |
| Halo-lit (reverse channel) reception logo | $6,500–$18,000 |
| Building or tenant directory, non-digital | $1,800–$9,000 |
| Digital directory with CMS | $6,000–$20,000 |
| Full program, 20,000 sf office floor | $18,000–$60,000 |

### What actually drives the number

**Illumination.** A halo-lit logo costs roughly three times its non-illuminated twin, and most of that gap is not the LEDs. It is the fabricated returns, the power drop, the licensed electrical tie-in, and the wall coordination that has to happen before drywall closes. Decide on illumination during design development, not after.

**Substrate and mounting.** Studs-and-spacers into stud-backed drywall is routine. The same letters on glass, stone, fabric-wrapped acoustic panel, or a metal-stud wall with no blocking behind it can double install labor. Blocking is nearly free at framing and expensive after.

**Letter depth and material.** Quarter-inch flat-cut acrylic is the low end. Half-inch to one-inch fabricated aluminum with a painted or brushed face is where corporate lobbies usually land, and it prices by the linear inch of return, not by the letter.

**Quantity.** ADA room signs price on a curve. Forty doors is a different unit cost than four.

### The ADA rules that set the spec

Every permanent room and space in a commercial interior needs tactile signage, and the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design are specific enough that they effectively write the spec sheet:

- Tactile characters must be **raised at least 1/32 inch**, uppercase and sans-serif (§703.2), and duplicated in **Grade 2 Braille** (§703.3).
- Tactile characters must sit **48 inches minimum** above the finished floor at the baseline of the lowest character and **60 inches maximum** at the baseline of the highest (§703.4.1).
- Where there is a door, the sign goes on the **latch side**, with an 18-by-18-inch clear approach outside the door swing (§703.4.2).
- Characters and backgrounds must be **non-glare** and contrast with each other — light on dark or dark on light (§703.5.1).

Florida enforces these through the Accessibility volume of the Florida Building Code, which incorporates the federal standards. A sign that reads beautifully and mounts at 44 inches fails inspection just as hard as one with no Braille at all.

### Permits: the Jacksonville reality

Jacksonville's sign regulations (Chapter 656, Part 13 of the Ordinance Code) attach to signs placed on the ground, on or outside a building, or on a window. Purely interior signage — reception logos, room IDs, directories, wall graphics not readable from outside — generally falls outside that permitting track.

Two caveats that catch people:

1. **Illuminated interior signs** involve an electrical tie-in that belongs on the tenant-improvement building permit, not on a separate sign permit.
2. **Anything readable through the storefront glass** — a logo aimed outward, a window graphic — crosses back into sign-code territory and is counted against your allowable sign area.

### Where Brand 9 Signs fits

Brand 9 Signs has fabricated and installed commercial signage out of Jacksonville since 1986, and interior branded environments are one of the shop's core service lines alongside monuments, wayfinding, and builder signage. The practical value of a single fabricator-installer on a branded-environment package is sequencing: the ADA package, the reception feature, the directory, and the glass film all get surveyed once, drawn once, and installed against one schedule that matches the general contractor's. Design-only firms hand you drawings; a fabricator hands you a wall.

If you are budgeting a build-out, get interior signage priced at design development. It is a small line item that becomes an expensive one only when it is scheduled last.

items.body_md:
South Florida community entrance signs generally cost **$18,000–$35,000** for an unlit stucco-and-CMU wall, **$45,000–$90,000** for an illuminated dual-wall entry with stone veneer and fabricated metal letters, and **$120,000–$400,000+** for a flagship gated entry with paired walls, guardhouse identification, and integrated landscape lighting.

In Miami Beach, Palm Beach, Naples, Marco Island and Key West, those numbers run roughly 20–35% above the same design in Jacksonville or Orlando. The gap is not coastal markup. It is four specific requirements that only apply once you cross into the hurricane, salt, and sea-turtle zones — and one of them changes on December 31, 2026.

## What South Florida community entrance signs cost

| Entrance type | Installed range | What drives it |
|---|---|---|
| Single unlit monument, stucco over CMU, applied acrylic letters | $18K–$35K | Footing depth, letter material |
| Illuminated single monument, stone veneer, halo-lit metal letters | $32K–$58K | Electrical run, transformer, letter fabrication |
| Dual-wall entry, both sides of an entry drive, illuminated | $45K–$90K | Two footings, two services, symmetry tolerance |
| Gated flagship entry with guardhouse ID and phase signage | $120K–$400K+ | Structural walls, coordination with civil |

Add separately: signed and sealed structural engineering ($2,500–$9,000), permit and impact fees ($800–$4,500 depending on jurisdiction), and electrical service to the monument, the most underestimated line item on a raw site — a 200-foot trenched run with a dedicated meter adds $6,000–$15,000 before anyone touches the sign.

## Why the same monument costs more below Palm Beach

### 1. HVHZ engineering (Miami-Dade and Broward)

Miami-Dade and Broward counties are Florida's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. A monument there is engineered to a 175 mph design wind speed in Miami-Dade and 170 mph in Broward, versus roughly 130 mph in Duval County. Collier County — Naples and Marco Island — enforces about 170 mph under its local override, and Monroe County runs to 180 mph down through Key West. Every figure here is Risk Category II, the normal classification for a monument sign. Pull the site-specific value for your coordinates — do not assume the county number.

Practically, higher pressure means a deeper and wider footing, more reinforcing steel, and thicker gauge on any fabricated cabinet or letter. The sign face doesn't change. The concrete below grade does, and that is where the cost lives.

### 2. Salt air rewrites the material spec

A coastal entry within a mile of open water should specify 316 stainless fasteners rather than 304, and any painted aluminum should carry an **AAMA 2605** coating — the 70% PVDF class rated for 10-year South Florida exposure — not the AAMA 2604 finish that is adequate inland. The upcharge is roughly 8–14% on the fabricated components and it is the difference between a monument that chalks in four years and one that still reads clean at twelve.

### 3. Marine turtle lighting is a hard constraint, not a preference

If the community sits in a coastal county's lighting zone, illumination has to comply with a local ordinance built on Florida's model rule, **Chapter 62B-55, F.A.C.** Three principles govern: keep it low, keep it long-wavelength, keep it shielded. Long wavelength means a source emitting at **560 nanometers or greater** — amber or red, never white LED. Nesting season is May 1 through October 31 in Collier, Lee, and Monroe, but runs **March 1 through October 31** in Palm Beach and Broward, which surprises developers phasing a Palm Beach or Miami Beach entry for a spring model-home opening. Naples, Marco Island and Key West sit on the May 1 calendar.

The usual answer is a shielded, ground-recessed, amber-filtered fixture aimed only at the sign face — or halo-lit letters, so the source is never visible from the beach.

### 4. The approval stack nobody budgets for

Before the county permit, a South Florida entrance monument typically clears an architectural review board or HOA design committee, and in a master-planned community, the **Community Development District** board under Chapter 190, F.S. If the entry meets a county or state road, add a right-of-way permit and a sight-triangle review. Sequential approvals, each on a monthly meeting cycle, are why a 6-week fabrication turns into a 5-month project.

## The permit timing that matters right now

Florida is currently on the **8th Edition (2023) Florida Building Code**. The **9th Edition takes effect December 31, 2026**, pulling from the 2024 I-Codes. Projects with a complete permit application on file before that date generally proceed under the 8th Edition. If a developer has a monument designed and engineered to current code, filing the application before year-end avoids a re-engineering cycle. That is a real deadline worth putting on a Q4 schedule.

## A five-line spec that protects the budget

1. Site-specific ASCE 7-22 wind speed and exposure category, from the actual coordinates.
2. Signed and sealed foundation design by a Florida PE, not a generic detail.
3. AAMA 2605 finish and 316 stainless hardware on anything within a mile of salt water.
4. Confirm the turtle-lighting zone and nesting-season dates before selecting fixtures.
5. Identify every approval body and their meeting calendars on day one.

Brand 9 Signs has fabricated and installed community entrance signage across Florida since 1986, from our Jacksonville shop. We build to the site's code, not a catalog — which on the coast means the engineering happens before the rendering.
